expectations.reason: Both parsers and renderers represent an exact millisecond UTC timestamp, decimal counter and ASCII node identifier.
Dart DateTime and toIso8601String preserve microseconds while JavaScript Date and toISOString retain milliseconds only (packages/ledger_engine/lib/src/hlc.dart; styx-js/src/ledger/hlc.js).

Dart projects canonical string code units into Uint8List while JavaScript applies UTF-8 TextEncoder, which differs for non-ASCII input (packages/ledger_engine/lib/src/hlc.dart; styx-js/src/ledger/hlc.js).
Dart int.parse rejects the counter while JavaScript parseInt produces NaN and the frozen object remains constructible.
Dart splits from the final two dashes; JavaScript treats the remainder after the first counter separator as the node identifier.
Both comparisons order the identical timestamp and node by the decimal counter.
Dart silently truncates the U+65E5 UTF-16 code unit to one byte while JavaScript TextEncoder emits its UTF-8 sequence.
Dart projects U+00E9 and U+01E9 to the same low byte while JavaScript UTF-8 preserves distinct scalar values; the witness is explicitly non-normative.
Both two-component implementations expose the same basic values, total and big-endian bytes in the positive signed range.
Dart signed int32 and JavaScript uint32 coercion yield the same two's-complement bytes for int32 maximum and minus one.
Dart 3.10.8 ByteData.setInt32 and JavaScript uint32BE both encode 2^31 as 80000000; the original rejection hypothesis was disproven by the isolated adapters.
Dart 3.10.8 ByteData.setInt32 and JavaScript bitwise conversion both wrap 2^32+5 to 00000005; the original rejection hypothesis was disproven by the isolated adapters.
Both increment implementations reject roles other than A or B; harness reason codes normalize only the error category.
Both implementations use component-wise maximum and the same two-component causal relation.
Both current constructors expose exactly two components and cannot express a third participant without production changes.
Both implementations increment role A while leaving role B unchanged.
Both implementations increment role B while leaving role A unchanged.
Both Hasher implementations apply SHA-256 to the identical empty byte string.
Both chainHash implementations hash only payload when previousHash is null.
Both compositeHash implementations concatenate the same ordered raw segments before SHA-256.
Both current compositeHash implementations erase segment boundaries; the match is explicitly marked unspecified and non-normative.
Both current compositeHash implementations erase an inserted empty segment; the match is explicitly marked unspecified and non-normative.
Both public computeHashBytes paths concatenate the same explicit previous-hash text, event type, payload and HLC bytes.
Current Dart and JavaScript createGenesisEvent paths choose different deterministic payloads and initial vector clocks.
Both public genesis constructors bind the hash to wall-clock HLC state and expose no deterministic clock injection without production changes.
Both ordering implementations sort first by vector-clock total.
Dart compares UTF-16 code units while JavaScript uses localeCompare for the equal-total sender tiebreak.
The non-ASCII sender is equal on both events, so the distinct vector-clock totals determine the order before string collation.
Both comparators return equality for the complete tie; the case remains explicitly unspecified because no shared stable-order guarantee exists.
Equal vector-clock totals force a non-ASCII sender tie-break: Dart compares UTF-16 code units while JavaScript uses default ICU collation.
Both validateFullChain implementations currently return success for an empty list; this is recorded only as an incompleteness witness.
Both validators reject a first event whose previousHash is non-null before cryptographic validation.
Both validators classify an incorrect stored hash as hashMismatch after the genesis-link check.
Both validators reach signature verification when the stored hash is implementation-correct and classify the all-zero signature as invalid.
Both validators reject a second event whose previousHash does not match the preceding event before hashing or signature verification.
Both full-chain validators accept the same independently derived one-event chain whose stored hash and RFC 8032 Ed25519 signature are supplied literally by the corpus.
